Field surveys of the bronze-striped grunt (Orthopristis reddingi) conducted in the Gulf of California have provided detailed morphometric data for this commercially valued haemulid. Juveniles captured in seagrass beds exhibit a modest body mass shortly after hatching, with newly emerged yolk-sac larvae weighing approximately 0.00032 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00032 grams]. This remarkably small neonatal mass is comparable to values observed in other haemulids and reflects the high fecundity characteristic of broadcast-spawning marine teleosts. The yolk-sac larval phase is brief, as these larvae quickly transition to exogenous feeding once yolk reserves are depleted and the mouth gapes sufficiently for first prey capture. Growth during the early juvenile period is relatively rapid, fueled by the abundant zooplankton present in these shallow nursery habitats. As individuals mature and recruit to deeper rocky reef environments, their growth trajectories begin to stabilize, gradually approaching the asymptotic dimensions typical of the adult population. The species exhibits pronounced sexual monomorphism in size, making external sex determination difficult without gonad inspection during the spawning season.

Upon reaching sexual maturation, O. reddingi individuals attain a total length at puberty of 15 centimeters [Lp = 15 centimeters]. This size threshold marks the onset of gonadal recrudescence and the initiation of reproductive activity. Puberty in this species is reached after a juvenile phase lasting several months, during which individuals accumulate sufficient energy reserves to support the metabolic demands of gametogenesis. At this life stage, the fish weigh approximately 100 grams [Wwp = approximately 100 grams], a mass that correlates well with the onset of vitellogenesis in females and spermiation in males. This body mass at puberty is relatively modest compared to the ultimate adult size, suggesting that individuals invest in reproduction early while still actively growing. Histological examination of gonadal tissue indicates that first-time spawners produce fewer gametes than older, more experienced conspecifics. The reproductive strategy appears to be iteroparous, with individuals capable of spawning multiple times across successive breeding seasons once they attain this critical length and weight threshold. Further growth continues steadily throughout the adult phase.

As adults approach their maximum asymptotic size, the bronze-striped grunt reaches an ultimate total length of 29.8 centimeters [Li = 29.8 centimeters]. This maximal length, derived from extensive length-frequency distributions of captured specimens, represents the largest individuals typically encountered within the population. Correspondingly, the ultimate wet weight attained by fully grown adults is approximately 600 grams [Wwi = approximately 600 grams], a value estimated from length-weight regressions applied to large-bodied individuals. This species does not exhibit the extreme size dimorphism seen in some serranids; rather, both sexes converge on similar maximum dimensions, a pattern common among schooling haemulids with pair-spawning behavior. The largest recorded specimens tend to be females, likely reflecting the energetic demands of producing large numbers of pelagic eggs each reproductive season. Data from otolith-based ageing studies indicate that these maximum sizes are achieved slowly, with individuals continuing to add somatic tissue for several years after reaching sexual maturity. Growth deceleration becomes evident once fish surpass approximately 400 grams, as energetic resources are increasingly redirected toward reproductive output.

The maximum reproductive output of O. reddingi has been characterized under controlled laboratory conditions at a stable water temperature of 22.3 °C [T = 22.3 °C], reflecting the typical thermal regime of its Gulf of California spawning grounds. Under these conditions, spawning females produce an average of approximately 600 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 600 eggs per spawning event], and they are capable of releasing up to approximately one spawning event each day [F_R_i = approximately one spawning event each day] during the peak of the reproductive season. This high-frequency spawning strategy, sustained over several weeks, allows females to achieve a substantial cumulative reproductive output. The daily batch fecundity extrapolates to a maximal annual production of several hundred thousand eggs per individual when integrated across the entire spawning period. This elevated reproductive capacity is typical of subtropical haemulids that experience a prolonged warm-water season, during which metabolic rates and gametogenic cycles remain accelerated. Peak spawning activity appears synchronized with the lunar cycle, with greatest spawning intensity observed around the new moon. The warm thermal conditions accelerate oocyte development and shorten the inter-spawn interval.

Longevity data derived from mark-recapture studies and otolith annuli analysis indicate that the bronze-striped grunt has a maximum recorded lifespan of approximately 12 years [am = approximately 12 years] when maintained at a mean annual water temperature of 22.3 °C [T = 22.3 °C]. This lifespan is relatively extended for a haemulid of this body size and suggests a comparatively slow pace of life, with sustained reproductive output possible over many seasons. Mortality rates are highest during the pelagic larval phase and early juvenile stages, but once individuals settle on reefs and attain a body size exceeding approximately 15 centimeters in length, predation pressure declines markedly. The oldest individuals in the population are generally those inhabiting deeper, more structurally complex rocky habitats that provide refuge from large piscivores such as groupers and sharks. Senescence in this species manifests as a gradual decline in body condition and gamete quality rather than a sudden post-reproductive collapse, consistent with an iteroparous life-history strategy. Population modelling efforts suggest that the combination of moderate longevity, high fecundity, and early maturation confers considerable resilience to moderate levels of fishing pressure.
